# CAD modeling and inspection

A model is a Python function that returns a build123d shape. Running its script builds it in
text-to-cad's server, which holds the result as a document: the page the person has open follows
every run, and every command (inspect, snapshot, export, check) acts on that document by its id.
Files are exports, written when asked.

## Start with the task

| Task | Start with | Reference |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Create or edit a part or assembly | A model script ([below](#write-a-model-and-run-it)) | [Models](references/model-contract.md), [build123d](references/build123d-modeling.md), [positioning](references/positioning.md) |
| Let the person tune a number (a wall, a fit, a count) | `model.param(...)` at the script's top level; change a value by editing its number and running the script | [Parameters](references/model-contract.md#parameters-a-person-tunes) |
| Organize a project | Its existing layout | [Project layout](references/project-layout.md) |
| Export STEP, STL, 3MF, GLB or xbf | `cad model export <id> <file>` | [Exports](references/exports.md) |
| A 2D profile, flat pattern or DXF | A model that returns 2D geometry on z=0, exported as `.dxf` | [2D profiles and DXF](references/2d-profiles-and-dxf.md) |
| Use a vendor STEP, an xbf or a scan | `step.read`, `xbf.read` or `stl.read` in the body | [Inputs](references/model-contract.md#inputs) |
| Resolve a reference or a Quick Edit prompt | `cad model inspect <id> '<ref>'` | [References](references/inspection-and-validation.md#references) |
| Measure or check geometry | A check script that calls the model | [Inspection](references/inspection-and-validation.md) |
| See a model, a view or a pose | `cad model snapshot <id> out.png` | [Snapshots](references/snapshot-review.md) |
| Articulate a mechanism, find joint limits | build123d joints in the body; `cad model ranges <id>` | [Kinematics](references/kinematics.md) |
| Explode, reveal or showcase a model | `animation()` in the body | [Animation](references/animation.md) |
| Can it be machined, bent, molded or printed? | `cad model dfm <id> --process ...` | [Can it be made?](#can-it-be-made) |
| Open an existing CAD file | Show it | [Show the model](#show-the-model) |

Whether a part holds under load is the fea skill's; a robot description, the robot-simulation skill's.

## Setup

Written for `cad==0.11.17`. Before first use in a chat, run `cad --version`. If `cad` is missing or older than
0.11.12, run `uv tool install cad`, adding `--force` if uv says `cad` already exists.

If cad is a major or minor version newer than this skill, tell the person to update the text-to-cad plugin:
https://github.com/earthtojake/text-to-cad
A project written for an earlier version may need changes; the migration guides say what:
https://github.com/earthtojake/text-to-cad/tree/main/docs/migrations

Every command goes through one server: start it once with `cad server start` (`status`, `stop`); a
command that finds none says so. `cad run script.py` is `uv run` with cad's library and the
integrations the script imports added, so a script header names only its own extra packages, never
cad ([environments](references/environments.md)). A
build outlives the shell's time limit: run the same command again and it joins the build in progress.
`cad <command> --help` is the complete, current interface. Paths are relative to the working
directory.

## Write a model and run it

`src/bracket.py`:

```python
import build123d as bd
from cad import model


def bracket_body(width, thickness, bore):
    body = bd.Box(width, 20, thickness) - bd.Cylinder(bore / 2, thickness)
    body.label = "bracket"
    body.color = "#4a6fa5"
    return body


@model
def bracket():
    return bracket_body(40, 6, 8)


@model
def bracket_wide():
    return bracket_body(60, 6, 8)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    bracket()
    bracket_wide()
```

```bash
cad run src/bracket.py
```

```text
built src/bracket.py::bracket cold in 2.61s: bodies 1 run; 6 misses, 0 hits; body 0.01s, names 0.00s, document 0.00s
  parts 1 · bounds 40 × 20 × 6 mm · joints 0 · sequences 0
  id: 0dc50a92-a21f-5895-a245-ebdeb5352f3b
  view: http://127.0.0.1:<port>/<id>?token=<token>
```

Each call prints how its model built, what it holds, its document's `id:` and its page, `view:`. The
id comes from the script's path and the function's name, so it is the same on every run: use it for
every command, and give the person the page once ([Show the model](#show-the-model)).

- **A model function takes no arguments.** Dimensions are arguments of a plain helper, and each
  configuration is a `@model` of its own. Calling one returns a handle: `.id`, `.url`, `.shape`, `.export(...)`.
- **Running the script is the rebuild**, and it writes no file. The server replays whatever an edit
  did not reach, so reruns are cheap; `@memo` marks a stage of seconds of kernel work, or a body several models share
  ([what a run runs](references/model-contract.md#what-a-run-runs)). Keep the calls under
  `if __name__ == "__main__":` so other scripts can import the models.
- **An assembly calls its parts**: its body takes each part's shape (`plate().shape`), places and
  labels it, and returns a `Compound`. Each part keeps its own document. After editing a part, run the
  assembly's script.
- **Use `import build123d as bd`, attribute-style.** The import is lazy, so the kernel loads in the
  server; `from build123d import Box` or a module-level `bd.Color(...)` loads it in the script.
- **Labels name parts** in every reference, check and export. Colours are sRGB hex
  (`part.color = "#4a6fa5"`); a material gives a part density and a look
  (`from bd_materials import metals`, `part.material = metals.aluminum()`:
  [colour and materials](references/build123d-modeling.md#colour-and-materials)).
- **A body is a function of its code and its inputs**: `step.read`, `xbf.read`, `stl.read` and any
  file it opens are tracked; the clock, environment variables and randomness are not. Compose project
  models by calling them, never by reading a file the project exported.
- Units are millimetres, +Z up.

## Commands

Each acts on the document as the last run left it. `$ID` is a model's id; a file takes the
operations its own type lists (`cad step|xbf|stl|threemf|glb|dxf --help`).

| Command | Gives |
| --- | --- |
| `cad model inspect "$ID" ['<ref>']` | The document's parts, bounds, volume, mass and joints; with a ref, one part, face or edge as JSON, with `made_by`: the function, file and line that made it |
| `cad model snapshot "$ID" out.png` | A picture, drawn as the viewer draws it: `--camera top`, `--display hidden-line`, `--pose open`, `--preview` (lit, for a person) |
| `cad model export "$ID" a.step b.stl c.glb` | Files, by suffix; nothing rebuilds ([exports](references/exports.md)) |
| `cad model interference "$ID" [--pose P]` | Every pair of parts that shares volume, exactly, as built and at each pose |
| `cad model dfm "$ID" --process ...` | A manufacturing check ([Can it be made?](#can-it-be-made)) |
| `cad model ranges "$ID"` | Each joint's stops, swept from the parts ([joint stops](references/kinematics.md#joint-stops)) |
| `cad step export vendor.step vendor.xbf` | A vendor STEP as an xbf, which `xbf.read` loads many times faster |

`--tolerance MM` and `--angle DEG` mesh an STL, a 3MF or a GLB finer (a print with fits, a close
render) and apply to nothing else: an export that takes them names only mesh files, and a STEP, xbf or
DXF beside them refuses the whole export.

```bash
cad model export "$ID" STEP/bracket.step GLB/bracket.glb
cad model export "$ID" STL/bracket.stl 3MF/bracket.3mf --tolerance 0.02
```

A reference such as `0dc50a92-...#bracket/face 7` is what the viewer copies when the person picks
something: a document, a part by its labels, then an element. Resolve it with `inspect`, then edit the
code `made_by` names. A Quick Edit prompt carries its document under `File:`, its picks under
`References:` and a snapshot packet, inline JSON (save it to a file) or a `.snapshot.json` path. Where
the person drew on the view, look at what they drew before editing:
`cad model snapshot "$ID" out.png --annotation packet.snapshot.json --camera authored`
([annotations](references/snapshot-review.md#annotations-and-quick-edit-views)).

## Check each change

Read each run's output first: a part count, bounds or joint count that contradicts the intent is the
first thing to fix. Then check the change the way it can be checked:

| The change | Check it with |
| --- | --- |
| A number the person gave (a size, a distance, a volume) | An assert in the model's body on what the geometry measures, or `cad model inspect` |
| A number the design implies (a clearance, a fit, a mass) | A check script that calls the model and measures what it returns ([inspection](references/inspection-and-validation.md)) |
| An assembly's parts or a joint's travel | `cad model interference "$ID"`, with a `--pose` for each mechanism state |
| Shape, placement, colour, a mechanism | The snapshots it takes to judge it, posed where it moves |
| A 2D profile or DXF | The export, which runs the drawing checks, then `cad dxf snapshot` of the file |
| A part made by a named process | Its manufacturing check ([below](#can-it-be-made)) |

- A snapshot shows arrangement and appearance; a number comes from the geometry, never from a picture.
- Review an assembly from the inside out: a part alone before it is placed, then the parts that move
  together, then a joint at both ends of its travel, and only then the whole, from behind as well as
  the front. A cover that half encloses what it covers is a few pixels of the whole model's picture
  and most of its own.
- A check that fails to run, or cannot decide, has shown nothing. Trust a check you wrote only once
  you have seen it fail on a planted fault of the kind it guards against. Boxes, mesh points and
  sampled distances pick the pairs worth measuring; the verdict is exact geometry.
- Say what a check cannot see beside what it passed: the poses it did not take, the pairs it could not
  measure, the path between two poses checked only at its ends.
- Dropping or shrinking a feature the person specified to get a build through is a different design:
  say so instead.
- A missing or conflicting dimension that changes the result is the person's to settle; a value
  chosen in its place is an assumption to report.

## Can it be made?

`cad model dfm` says whether a part can be made by a process and what to change where it cannot. Run
it when the request names or implies a process (machined, sheet metal or laser cut, injection molded,
3D printed, or a printer, resin, filament or cutting service named), or the person asks. A material
alone names no process, but a thickness with a metal ("2 mm steel") is sheet. With none, build what was asked: no check, and no draft, reliefs or tool radii
added.

| Process | Check | Reference |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CNC milling and turning | `--process cnc --material M` (`--axes`, `--turning`, `--tools`) | [CNC](references/manufacturing-cnc.md) |
| Sheet cutting and bending | `--process sheet --material M --thickness T` (`--bend-radius`, `--k-factor`); a cut file, `cad dxf dfm` | [Sheet metal](references/manufacturing-sheet-metal.md) |
| Injection molding | `--process molding --pull z --material M` (`--cavities`) | [Injection molding](references/manufacturing-injection-molding.md) |
| 3D printing | `--process printing --technology T` (`--material`, `--build-volume`, `--layer-height`) | [3D printing](references/manufacturing-printing.md) |

```bash
cad model dfm "$ID" --process cnc --material aluminum --tools 3,6,10
```

A named process is part of the design, not a review at the end:

1. Read the process reference's *Design it* before modelling, and build its limits in.
2. Record the process in the model, so every later check is the same one: the material with its
   process on each part (`part.material = metals.aluminum(process=machined())`, with `machined` from
   `bd_materials.processes`), and the shop's flags in the module docstring
   (`Check: cad model dfm "$ID" --tools 3,6,10`).
3. Run that check after every run. The last line and the exit status are the result: `OK` (0, though
   warnings may remain), `FAILED` (1: the part cannot be made as drawn), `NOT CHECKED` (3: something
   was not judged, never a pass) and 2 for a refused command. Fix errors from each finding's `refs`,
   `value` and `limit` (`--json`); fix a warning when that leaves the request intact, else report it.
4. In the hand-off, say the process, the material the check judged with, the findings left, and that
   the rules are general practice rather than a shop's own limits.

A STEP or mesh file is checked by its own type (`cad step dfm part.step --process ...`); a mesh, for
printing only. For a review, a shop's own limits or the result in full, read
[manufacturing review](references/manufacturing-review.md). A SendCutSend order is the sendcutsend
skill's; slicing a print, the print3d skill's.

## Show the model

Show the person each model you create or change as soon as its first run succeeds, and any model
or file they ask to see. A model's page is the `view:` line its run prints, and a file's is the `url`
that `cad viewer --json FILE [FILE ...]` prints for it (never guess the port). Show it with
the first of these you have:

1. `cad_show` among your tools (your host may prefix it): call it with the model's id or the file's
   absolute path; its description says the rest.
2. A tool that opens a page in the app's own browser pane, not in the person's own browser (in the
   Claude desktop app, the Browser pane's `preview_start` with the page's `url`, or its `navigate`):
   open the page there yourself, and give the person the link as well.
3. Neither: give the person the link, to open in their browser.

The page follows every run of the model. A file you export is a download: give its path. Showing is
for the person: to check your own work, review with `cad <type> snapshot`, never a screenshot
of the page. If it fails to launch, say so.

## Hand off

Say what was made or changed, the files written, the checks run and what they showed, what no check
covered, and every assumption or departure from the request.

2. Record the process in the model, so every later check is the same one: the material with its
   process on each part (`part.material = metals.aluminum(process=machined())`, with `machined` from
   `bd_materials.processes`), and the shop's flags in the module docstring
   (`Check: cad model dfm "$ID" --tools 3,6,10`).
3. Run that check after every run. The last line and the exit status are the result: `OK` (0, though
   warnings may remain), `FAILED` (1: the part cannot be made as drawn), `NOT CHECKED` (3: something
   was not judged, never a pass) and 2 for a refused command. Fix errors from each finding's `refs`,
   `value` and `limit` (`--json`); fix a warning when that leaves the request intact, else report it.
4. In the hand-off, say the process, the material the check judged with, the findings left, and that
   the rules are general practice rather than a shop's own limits.

printing only. For a review, a shop's own limits or the result in full, read
[manufacturing review](references/manufacturing-review.md). A SendCutSend order is the sendcutsend
skill's; slicing a print, the print3d skill's.

## Show the model

Show the person each model you create or change as soon as its first run succeeds, and any model
or file they ask to see. A model's page is the `view:` line its run prints, and a file's is the `url`
that `cad viewer --json FILE [FILE ...]` prints for it (never guess the port). Show it with
the first of these you have:

1. `cad_show` among your tools (your host may prefix it): call it with the model's id or the file's
   absolute path; its description says the rest.
2. A tool that opens a page in the app's own browser pane, not in the person's own browser (in the
   Claude desktop app, the Browser pane's `preview_start` with the page's `url`, or its `navigate`):
   open the page there yourself, and give the person the link as well.
3. Neither: give the person the link, to open in their browser.

for the person: to check your own work, review with `cad <type> snapshot`, never a screenshot
of the page. If it fails to launch, say so.

## Hand off

Say what was made or changed, the files written, the checks run and what they showed, what no check
covered, and every assumption or departure from the request.

# Engineering drawing

An engineering drawing is a document derived from a part. `cad.eng_drawing` projects views from the
part's geometry, places dimensions between points on that geometry, finds centre marks, and lays the
result out on an ISO sheet with a frame and a title block. Change the model and rerun the drawing
script, and the views, hidden lines and measured values follow.

The output is one PDF, written by a Python script: there is no command and no DXF. A cut layout or a
flat pattern is a toolpath, not a document: that is the cad skill's.

## Start with the task

| Task | Start with | Reference |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Draw a part | `<name>_drawing.py` beside the model, from the script under [Workflow](#workflow) | [The calls](references/sheet-api.md) |
| Place views, dimensions, hole callouts, notes | `Sheet` and `View` | [Sheet API](references/sheet-api.md) |
| Check the drawing | What the run prints, then the PDF itself | [Check each change](#check-each-change) |

## Setup

Written for `cad==0.11.17`. Before first use in a chat, run `cad --version`. If `cad` is missing or older than
0.11.12, run `uv tool install cad`, adding `--force` if uv says `cad` already exists.

If cad is a major or minor version newer than this skill, tell the person to update the text-to-cad plugin:
https://github.com/earthtojake/text-to-cad
A project written for an earlier version may need changes; the migration guides say what:
https://github.com/earthtojake/text-to-cad/tree/main/docs/migrations

## Workflow

```python
from cad.eng_drawing import Sheet, eng_drawing
from enclosure import HOLES, L, H, W, enclosure   # the part and its facts come from the model


@eng_drawing(out="../PDF/enclosure_drawing.pdf")
def enclosure_drawing():
    part = enclosure().shape
    sheet = Sheet("A3", title="ENCLOSURE", part_number="ENC-001", material="ABS",
                  revision="A", general_tolerance="ISO 2768-m", notes=["BREAK SHARP EDGES."])
    top, front, right, iso = sheet.three_views(part, iso=True)
    top.overall()
    top.dim((HOLES[0][0], W / 2, 0), (HOLES[2][0], W / 2, 0))
    top.hole((HOLES[3][0], HOLES[3][1], H / 2), 3, depth=8, count=len(HOLES))
    front.dim((L / 2, -W / 2, 0), (L / 2, -W / 2, H))
    return sheet


if __name__ == "__main__":
    enclosure_drawing()
```

```bash
cad run enclosure_drawing.py
```

1. **Get the part.** Call the model and take its `.shape`; for a part with no model, read its file
   (`step.read`, `xbf.read`, the path anchored on `Path(__file__).parent`). Any build123d shape works.
2. **Import the model's facts** (hole pitch, overall size, wall) instead of retyping them, so moving a
   feature moves its dimension.
3. **Place views.** `sheet.three_views(part, iso=True)` returns four views: top, front and right in
   third angle with room for two rows of dimensions, and an isometric in the free corner (three
   without `iso`). `sheet.view(part, name, at=(x, y))` is for a custom layout, in sheet millimetres
   from the bottom-left corner.
4. **Dimension what a maker needs**, in model coordinates: overall size (`view.overall()`), feature
   positions and sizes (`view.dim`, with `tol=` or `fit=` where the design requires one), holes as
   callouts (`view.hole`: thru, depth, counterbore, countersink, thread) and notes with leaders
   (`view.note`). Leave `text` unset so the value is measured, and `offset` unset so the dimension
   takes the next free row outside the view.
5. **Run it and read the PDF.**

## Check each change

The run prints the PDF it wrote and anything it noticed while drawing. Read those first:

- **"measures blank paper"**: a dimension's model points do not land on the view's geometry. Usually
  the part was built from a corner and the script assumed it was centred: check its bounding box.
- **"annotation overlaps"**: two callouts print over each other, usually one view's outermost
  dimension against the label of the view above. Pass a larger `three_views(gap=...)` or place one
  with `offset=`.

Then open the PDF. The sheet keeps callouts clear of the views and reports annotation over
annotation, but it does not check annotation against line work: confirm no dimension text sits on a
view, hidden lines appear where features are behind faces, every hole has a centre mark, and no
leader crosses the part. A dimension of a few millimetres puts its value on its own extension line:
dimension the larger feature instead.

The script raises instead of writing a wrong or partial document: views that run off the frame (the
error names a scale that fits, or says that none does), an argument outside the vocabulary (an
unknown view, sheet size or projection; a hole both `thru` and given a depth; `notes=` given a bare
string instead of a list; a note wider than the sheet's note column), or a missing renderer. A failed
run leaves any earlier PDF untouched.

## What the drawing holds, and what it does not

- Visible edges heavy, hidden edges dashed, centre marks, dimensions with witness lines and
  arrowheads at true size at any drawing scale, and a title block (title, part number, material,
  scale, projection, revision, `SHEET n OF m`) with numbered notes above it. Text longer than its
  title-block cell is set smaller, then cut with an ellipsis, and nothing says so: read the title
  block in the PDF. Hidden tangent edges (a fillet running into a face) are not drawn.
- The PDF's bytes are a function of its content, with no creation date: an unchanged drawing rebuilds
  to an identical file.
- **Tolerances are only the ones written** (`tol=`, `fit=`, `general_tolerance=`), from the design's
  requirements or the person, never invented. A dimension without one is nominal.
- **Views are orthographic projections**: no sections, details or auxiliary views. Say in the hand-off
  what a view does not show.

# FEA: will it hold, and how far does it move

A study holds some faces of a part, loads others, and solves the linear elastic response: stress and
displacement under forces, pressures, the part's own weight and steady accelerations, with an
isotropic material below yield, rigid fixtures and loads that do not move. An assembly's parts are
bonded where they touch. It is a first-pass engineering check, not a certification: say so in the
report. Vibration, buckling, heat, fatigue, impact and sliding contact are outside it, and a static
safety factor is no answer to them (a drop or a braking load can be estimated as a steady g-load:
[body loads](references/linear-static.md#body-loads-gravity-and-acceleration)).

## Start with the task

| Task | Start with | Reference |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Check a part under a load | `cad step solve part.step` lists its faces; write the study; solve into a folder | [Workflow](#workflow), [linear static](references/linear-static.md) |
| Check an assembly | `cad step solve assembly.step` lists the parts and the pairs that touch | [Assemblies](#assemblies) |
| Write or edit a study | One JSON object: fixtures and loads, then material, mesh, margin and checks | [Study file](references/study-file.md) |
| Choose a material | The model's own, or the E, ν and yield the person gives | [Materials](references/materials.md) |
| Judge the answer | `result.json` and its findings, against a hand estimate | [Findings](#findings), [judging the answer](references/linear-static.md#judging-the-answer) |
| Find the load a part takes | Solve at any load: the model is linear, so yield comes at the loads applied, all scaled by the safety factor | [`checks`](references/study-file.md#checks) |
| Answer what the summary does not | `result.vtu`, read with meshio | [Your own questions](#your-own-questions) |
| Compare design variants | The same study on each, faces mapped, mesh size held | [Compare variants](#compare-variants) |

The study reads a saved `.step` or `.xbf`, or a model the server holds by its id
(`cad model solve <id>`), and solves the whole document: to study one part of an assembly alone,
export it as a document of its own.

## Setup

Written for `cad==0.11.17`. Before first use in a chat, run `cad --version`. If `cad` is missing or older than
0.11.12, run `uv tool install cad`, adding `--force` if uv says `cad` already exists.

If cad is a major or minor version newer than this skill, tell the person to update the text-to-cad plugin:
https://github.com/earthtojake/text-to-cad
A project written for an earlier version may need changes; the migration guides say what:
https://github.com/earthtojake/text-to-cad/tree/main/docs/migrations

The mesher and the solver are fetched by `cad` the first time a study needs them, nothing to install:
the `netgen` integration (`cad[netgen]`, about 11 MB; macOS, Linux x86_64 and Windows x86_64 only, and
a solve elsewhere refuses, naming the platform) and the `calculix` integration (`cad[calculix]`,
CalculiX 2.23, about 13 MB). The solve runs headless on one thread, so the same study gives the same
numbers on every run. `cad run ccx ARGS` runs the same `ccx` on a deck of your own. A `ccx` on PATH is
never run; where the fetched one does not run on a computer, `CAD_CCX` names another (2.20 or newer).

Units are fixed: mm, N, MPa (pressure, modulus and stress), t/mm³ for density (steel 7.85e-9) and g
(9.81 m/s²) for gravity and acceleration. Restate every load in them before writing it down.

## Workflow

1. **List the faces.** With no study, `solve` prints the setup and writes nothing: the parts, the
   pairs that touch, then each face with its ref, area, centre, surface type and a hint such as
   `plane, normal -Z, largest`.

   ```bash
   cad step solve part.step
   ```

   Match the person's words ("the mounting face") to a ref by the hint and the centre; a hole is a
   `cylinder`. A face they picked in the viewer arrives as a ref already
   (`/work/bracket.step#bracket/face 17`). A document of several parts lists faces once one is named
   (`--occurrence post`). A face number is a position in the saved document, so list again after the
   part is edited.

2. **Write the study** ([study file](references/study-file.md)):

   ```json
   {
     "fixtures": [{"faces": ["bracket/face 17"], "type": "fixed"}],
     "loads": [{"faces": ["bracket/face 22"], "type": "force", "vector_N": [0, -500, 0]}]
   }
   ```

   `fixed` holds a face still; `roller` lets it slide in its plane (a frictionless support, a symmetry
   cut). A `force` is the total over its faces; a `pressure` is in MPa, positive into the surface;
   `gravity` and `acceleration` take `vector_g` and no faces, and need the material's density.
   `margin` is the safety factor the part should keep (default 2). `checks` adds a `displacement`
   limit when the person gave one. Leave `mesh` out on the first run.

3. **Solve into a folder**, one per study:

   ```bash
   cad step solve part.step --study study.json --out /tmp/bracket-load --json
   ```

   | File | What it is for |
   | --- | --- |
   | `result.json` | The answer, which `--json` also prints. Read this first |
   | `stress.png`, `displacement.png` | The deformed part coloured by each field, the deformation exaggerated by `deformation_scale`. They show whether the load points the way you meant and which faces are held |
   | `result.glb` | The same coloured surface, for `cad viewer` or any glTF viewer |
   | `result.vtu` | The volume mesh with `displacement` (mm) and `von_mises` (MPa) at its corner nodes |
   | `ccx.inp` | With `--deck`: the input CalculiX solved, to run or edit yourself (`cad run ccx -i ccx`, in that folder) |

   `result.json` holds `ok`, `findings` and `measurements`: the peak stress and where
   (`max_von_mises_MPa`, `max_von_mises_at_mm`), `yield_MPa`, `safety_factor`,
   `max_displacement_mm`, the applied force against the reactions, the mesh, and `refined` when the
   run solved twice ([what comes out](references/study-file.md#what-comes-out)).

   - A safety factor under 3 makes the run mesh finer and solve again by itself; the finer result is
     the one written ([mesh](references/linear-static.md#mesh)).
   - A malformed study is refused before meshing, naming the field. A part free to move, a load that
     reaches nothing, or reactions that do not balance the load are refused by the solve.
   - The exit status is 1 when a finding is an error (the part yields or misses a check, results
     written all the same; or `not_connected`, nothing written). Warnings leave it at 0.
   - Where the server cannot draw (Linux with no display) the pictures are left out and a
     `solver_note` says so.

4. **Report with units**: the peak von Mises and the feature it is near, the safety factor and the
   yield it is against, the largest displacement and where, the applied load against the reaction,
   the mesh size and whether a finer solve ran; then the findings, what the model assumes and what
   would change the answer most. Show `stress.png`, saying its deformation is exaggerated.

## Your own questions

For what the summary does not answer (the stress at the mounting holes, the sag along an edge, how
much of the part is above some stress), read `result.vtu` rather than solving again:

```python
# cad run --with meshio read-stress.py
import meshio, numpy as np

mesh = meshio.read("/tmp/bracket-load/result.vtu")
xyz, stress = mesh.points, mesh.point_data["von_mises"]          # mm, MPa
moved = np.linalg.norm(mesh.point_data["displacement"], axis=1)  # mm
near = np.linalg.norm(xyz - [42, 12, 3], axis=1) < 5             # within 5 mm of a point
print(stress[near].max(), moved[xyz[:, 2] > 49].max())
```

It holds the tetrahedra's corner nodes, inside the part as well as on its skin. The reported peak
also counts mid-edge nodes, so it can be a little above the VTU's maximum. An assembly's cells carry
their `part`, the index into the summary's `parts`.

## Assemblies

A document of several parts is solved as one: parts that touch are bonded into one mesh, each keeps
its own material, and each is judged against its own yield. Every part must reach a fixed part
through bonded neighbours ([study file](references/study-file.md#assemblies)).

- **Read the setup against the design.** It lists each pair as `bonded` (with its contact area and
  gap), `not connected` (a near miss, up to 1 mm), or `overlapping` (never bonded, unless the overlap
  is within the tolerance: an interference, bonded and closed like a gap). Is each detected joint
  real, and is an expected one missing? A wider gap is bonded by setting `contact_tolerance_mm`
  (default 0.1).
- **Materials**: each part uses its model's own; `parts` in the study gives one the person's numbers;
  a part with neither is refused by name.
- **`connections`** only overrides a detection (`free` for a pair that must not be glued). Parts that
  press, slide or are bolted are not modelled.
- **Faces** are named on any part (`post/face 23`), by its ref where names repeat (`frame/bar.2`). A
  face wholly covered by a bonded joint cannot be held or loaded.
- **Reading the result**: `yield_MPa` and `safety_factor` are the weakest part's (`weakest_part`),
  while `max_von_mises_MPa` and `max_displacement_mm` span the assembly, so never divide one by the
  other; each part's own numbers are in `parts`. Each finding names its part: fix that part.

## Compare variants

Each version of a design is its own document: run the same study on each into its own folder and
compare the `result.json`s. Face numbers are not stable between versions, and a ref reused unchecked
lands on a different face with no error, so list each variant's faces and map the baseline's by
surface type, normal, centre and area. Hold `mesh.size_mm` at the baseline's so a difference is the
design's and not the mesh's, and give the mapping with the table so the person can check it.

## Findings

Two von Mises peaks are reported. The **nodal** peak (`max_von_mises_MPa`, the one the safety factor
uses) is extrapolated from each element's integration points to its nodes and averaged; it is usually
the higher of the two. The **integration-point** peak (`max_von_mises_gauss_MPa`) is the raw element
value: more than 50 % above the nodal one, it means a concentration the mesh has not resolved. The
edge of a rigid fixture or bonded joint and a sharp inside corner are singularities, where the peak
grows with every refinement and never converges: read the stress a little away from them.

An error makes the part unfit as modelled; a warning is a judgment to weigh and explain. Most carry
the face and the point in mm.

| Finding | Severity | Means | Do |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `yields` | error | The nodal peak is above yield | Strengthen where the peak is, change the material, or confirm the load. A `peak_at_fixture` or `peak_concentration` beside it comes first: the peak may be the model's, not the part's |
| `low_margin` | warning | It holds, but under the study's `margin` | As for `yields`, or report the margin it has. Never lower `margin` to clear it |
| `displacement_over_limit` | error | A `displacement` check is past its `limit_mm` | Stiffen the part, or confirm the limit |
| `peak_at_fixture` | warning | The peak sits on a fixed face or its edge, and a finer solve did not settle it | Read the stress a little away from the face before redesigning |
| `peak_concentration` | warning | The integration-point peak is well above the nodal one: a sharp corner or concentrated load | Fillet the corner or spread the load. Under a safety factor of 3 the run already refined once; above it (a high `margin`), refine once yourself and compare |
| `mesh_not_converged` | warning | The finer solve moved the peak by more than 10 % | A peak that keeps rising is a singularity: fillet it or judge away from it. Otherwise set a smaller `mesh.size_mm` |
| `large_displacement` | warning | It moves more than 1 % of its size: the small-displacement model is stretched | Check the fit against mating parts; stiffen if the deflection matters |
| `not_connected` | error | A part has no bonded chain to a fixed part; nothing was solved | Make the parts touch, fix a face on the group, or raise `contact_tolerance_mm` |
| `overlapping_parts` | warning | Two solids overlap beyond the tolerance and are not bonded | Fix the geometry, or mark the pair `free` when the overlap is an accepted shortcut |
| `gap_closed` | warning | Two parts within the tolerance were bonded by moving geometry that far | Confirm it is a modelling clearance; the stress at that joint is the closing's, not the part's |
| `bonded_edge_peak` | warning | The peak sits on the edge of a bonded joint | Read the stress a little away; a bolted or welded joint is softer than this model |
| `solver_note` | warning | About the run: a slow solve, a finer solve skipped, pictures not drawn | Mention it when it bears on the answer |

`peak_at_fixture` and `peak_concentration` appear only when the safety factor is under the `margin`
and no finer solve settled the peak.

# FEA: will it hold, and how far does it move

A study holds some faces of a part, loads others, and solves the linear elastic response: stress and
displacement under forces, pressures, the part's own weight and steady accelerations, with an
isotropic material below yield, rigid fixtures and loads that do not move. An assembly's parts are
bonded where they touch. It is a first-pass engineering check, not a certification: say so in the
report. Vibration, buckling, heat, fatigue, impact and sliding contact are outside it, and a static
safety factor is no answer to them (a drop or a braking load can be estimated as a steady g-load:
[body loads](references/linear-static.md#body-loads-gravity-and-acceleration)).

## Start with the task

| Task | Start with | Reference |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Check a part under a load | `cad step solve part.step` lists its faces; write the study; solve into a folder | [Workflow](#workflow), [linear static](references/linear-static.md) |
| Check an assembly | `cad step solve assembly.step` lists the parts and the pairs that touch | [Assemblies](#assemblies) |
| Write or edit a study | One JSON object: fixtures and loads, then material, mesh, margin and checks | [Study file](references/study-file.md) |
| Choose a material | The model's own, or the E, ν and yield the person gives | [Materials](references/materials.md) |
| Judge the answer | `result.json` and its findings, against a hand estimate | [Findings](#findings), [judging the answer](references/linear-static.md#judging-the-answer) |
| Find the load a part takes | Solve at any load: the model is linear, so yield comes at the loads applied, all scaled by the safety factor | [`checks`](references/study-file.md#checks) |
| Answer what the summary does not | `result.vtu`, read with meshio | [Your own questions](#your-own-questions) |
| Compare design variants | The same study on each, faces mapped, mesh size held | [Compare variants](#compare-variants) |

The study reads a saved `.step` or `.xbf`, or a model the server holds by its id
(`cad model solve <id>`), and solves the whole document: to study one part of an assembly alone,
export it as a document of its own.

## Setup

Written for `cad==0.11.17`. Before first use in a chat, run `cad --version`. If `cad` is missing or older than
0.11.12, run `uv tool install cad`, adding `--force` if uv says `cad` already exists.

If cad is a major or minor version newer than this skill, tell the person to update the text-to-cad plugin:
https://github.com/earthtojake/text-to-cad
A project written for an earlier version may need changes; the migration guides say what:
https://github.com/earthtojake/text-to-cad/tree/main/docs/migrations

The mesher and the solver are fetched by `cad` the first time a study needs them, nothing to install:
the `netgen` integration (`cad[netgen]`, about 11 MB; macOS, Linux x86_64 and Windows x86_64 only, and
a solve elsewhere refuses, naming the platform) and the `calculix` integration (`cad[calculix]`,
CalculiX 2.23, about 13 MB). The solve runs headless on one thread, so the same study gives the same
numbers on every run. `cad run ccx ARGS` runs the same `ccx` on a deck of your own. A `ccx` on PATH is
never run; where the fetched one does not run on a computer, `CAD_CCX` names another (2.20 or newer).

Units are fixed: mm, N, MPa (pressure, modulus and stress), t/mm³ for density (steel 7.85e-9) and g
(9.81 m/s²) for gravity and acceleration. Restate every load in them before writing it down.

## Workflow

1. **List the faces.** With no study, `solve` prints the setup and writes nothing: the parts, the
   pairs that touch, then each face with its ref, area, centre, surface type and a hint such as
   `plane, normal -Z, largest`.

   ```bash
   cad step solve part.step
   ```

   Match the person's words ("the mounting face") to a ref by the hint and the centre; a hole is a
   `cylinder`. A face they picked in the viewer arrives as a ref already
   (`/work/bracket.step#bracket/face 17`). A document of several parts lists faces once one is named
   (`--occurrence post`). A face number is a position in the saved document, so list again after the
   part is edited.

2. **Write the study** ([study file](references/study-file.md)):

   ```json
   {
     "fixtures": [{"faces": ["bracket/face 17"], "type": "fixed"}],
     "loads": [{"faces": ["bracket/face 22"], "type": "force", "vector_N": [0, -500, 0]}]
   }
   ```

   `fixed` holds a face still; `roller` lets it slide in its plane (a frictionless support, a symmetry
   cut). A `force` is the total over its faces; a `pressure` is in MPa, positive into the surface;
   `gravity` and `acceleration` take `vector_g` and no faces, and need the material's density.
   `margin` is the safety factor the part should keep (default 2). `checks` adds a `displacement`
   limit when the person gave one. Leave `mesh` out on the first run.

3. **Solve into a folder**, one per study:

   ```bash
   cad step solve part.step --study study.json --out /tmp/bracket-load --json
   ```

   | File | What it is for |
   | --- | --- |
   | `result.json` | The answer, which `--json` also prints. Read this first |
   | `stress.png`, `displacement.png` | The deformed part coloured by each field, the deformation exaggerated by `deformation_scale`. They show whether the load points the way you meant and which faces are held |
   | `result.glb` | The same coloured surface, for `cad viewer` or any glTF viewer |
   | `result.vtu` | The volume mesh with `displacement` (mm) and `von_mises` (MPa) at its corner nodes |
   | `ccx.inp` | With `--deck`: the input CalculiX solved, to run or edit yourself (`cad run ccx -i ccx`, in that folder) |

   `result.json` holds `ok`, `findings` and `measurements`: the peak stress and where
   (`max_von_mises_MPa`, `max_von_mises_at_mm`), `yield_MPa`, `safety_factor`,
   `max_displacement_mm`, the applied force against the reactions, the mesh, and `refined` when the
   run solved twice ([what comes out](references/study-file.md#what-comes-out)).

   - A safety factor under 3 makes the run mesh finer and solve again by itself; the finer result is
     the one written ([mesh](references/linear-static.md#mesh)).
   - A malformed study is refused before meshing, naming the field. A part free to move, a load that
     reaches nothing, or reactions that do not balance the load are refused by the solve.
   - The exit status is 1 when a finding is an error (the part yields or misses a check, results
     written all the same; or `not_connected`, nothing written). Warnings leave it at 0.
   - Where the server cannot draw (Linux with no display) the pictures are left out and a
     `solver_note` says so.

4. **Report with units**: the peak von Mises and the feature it is near, the safety factor and the
   yield it is against, the largest displacement and where, the applied load against the reaction,
   the mesh size and whether a finer solve ran; then the findings, what the model assumes and what
   would change the answer most. Show `stress.png`, saying its deformation is exaggerated.

## Your own questions

For what the summary does not answer (the stress at the mounting holes, the sag along an edge, how
much of the part is above some stress), read `result.vtu` rather than solving again:

```python
# cad run --with meshio read-stress.py
import meshio, numpy as np

mesh = meshio.read("/tmp/bracket-load/result.vtu")
xyz, stress = mesh.points, mesh.point_data["von_mises"]          # mm, MPa
moved = np.linalg.norm(mesh.point_data["displacement"], axis=1)  # mm
near = np.linalg.norm(xyz - [42, 12, 3], axis=1) < 5             # within 5 mm of a point
print(stress[near].max(), moved[xyz[:, 2] > 49].max())
```

It holds the tetrahedra's corner nodes, inside the part as well as on its skin. The reported peak
also counts mid-edge nodes, so it can be a little above the VTU's maximum. An assembly's cells carry
their `part`, the index into the summary's `parts`.

## Assemblies

A document of several parts is solved as one: parts that touch are bonded into one mesh, each keeps
its own material, and each is judged against its own yield. Every part must reach a fixed part
through bonded neighbours ([study file](references/study-file.md#assemblies)).

- **Read the setup against the design.** It lists each pair as `bonded` (with its contact area and
  gap), `not connected` (a near miss, up to 1 mm), or `overlapping` (never bonded, unless the overlap
  is within the tolerance: an interference, bonded and closed like a gap). Is each detected joint
  real, and is an expected one missing? A wider gap is bonded by setting `contact_tolerance_mm`
  (default 0.1).
- **Materials**: each part uses its model's own; `parts` in the study gives one the person's numbers;
  a part with neither is refused by name.
- **`connections`** only overrides a detection (`free` for a pair that must not be glued). Parts that
  press, slide or are bolted are not modelled.
- **Faces** are named on any part (`post/face 23`), by its ref where names repeat (`frame/bar.2`). A
  face wholly covered by a bonded joint cannot be held or loaded.
- **Reading the result**: `yield_MPa` and `safety_factor` are the weakest part's (`weakest_part`),
  while `max_von_mises_MPa` and `max_displacement_mm` span the assembly, so never divide one by the
  other; each part's own numbers are in `parts`. Each finding names its part: fix that part.

## Compare variants

Each version of a design is its own document: run the same study on each into its own folder and
compare the `result.json`s. Face numbers are not stable between versions, and a ref reused unchecked
lands on a different face with no error, so list each variant's faces and map the baseline's by
surface type, normal, centre and area. Hold `mesh.size_mm` at the baseline's so a difference is the
design's and not the mesh's, and give the mapping with the table so the person can check it.

## Findings

Two von Mises peaks are reported. The **nodal** peak (`max_von_mises_MPa`, the one the safety factor
uses) is extrapolated from each element's integration points to its nodes and averaged; it is usually
the higher of the two. The **integration-point** peak (`max_von_mises_gauss_MPa`) is the raw element
value: more than 50 % above the nodal one, it means a concentration the mesh has not resolved. The
edge of a rigid fixture or bonded joint and a sharp inside corner are singularities, where the peak
grows with every refinement and never converges: read the stress a little away from them.

An error makes the part unfit as modelled; a warning is a judgment to weigh and explain. Most carry
the face and the point in mm.

| Finding | Severity | Means | Do |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `yields` | error | The nodal peak is above yield | Strengthen where the peak is, change the material, or confirm the load. A `peak_at_fixture` or `peak_concentration` beside it comes first: the peak may be the model's, not the part's |
| `low_margin` | warning | It holds, but under the study's `margin` | As for `yields`, or report the margin it has. Never lower `margin` to clear it |
| `displacement_over_limit` | error | A `displacement` check is past its `limit_mm` | Stiffen the part, or confirm the limit |
| `peak_at_fixture` | warning | The peak sits on a fixed face or its edge, and a finer solve did not settle it | Read the stress a little away from the face before redesigning |
| `peak_concentration` | warning | The integration-point peak is well above the nodal one: a sharp corner or concentrated load | Fillet the corner or spread the load. Under a safety factor of 3 the run already refined once; above it (a high `margin`), refine once yourself and compare |
| `mesh_not_converged` | warning | The finer solve moved the peak by more than 10 % | A peak that keeps rising is a singularity: fillet it or judge away from it. Otherwise set a smaller `mesh.size_mm` |
| `large_displacement` | warning | It moves more than 1 % of its size: the small-displacement model is stretched | Check the fit against mating parts; stiffen if the deflection matters |
| `not_connected` | error | A part has no bonded chain to a fixed part; nothing was solved | Make the parts touch, fix a face on the group, or raise `contact_tolerance_mm` |
| `overlapping_parts` | warning | Two solids overlap beyond the tolerance and are not bonded | Fix the geometry, or mark the pair `free` when the overlap is an accepted shortcut |
| `gap_closed` | warning | Two parts within the tolerance were bonded by moving geometry that far | Confirm it is a modelling clearance; the stress at that joint is the closing's, not the part's |
| `bonded_edge_peak` | warning | The peak sits on the edge of a bonded joint | Read the stress a little away; a bolted or welded joint is softer than this model |
| `solver_note` | warning | About the run: a slow solve, a finer solve skipped, pictures not drawn | Mention it when it bears on the answer |

`peak_at_fixture` and `peak_concentration` appear only when the safety factor is under the `margin`
and no finer solve settled the peak.

# PCB design

A board is its native KiCad files: the `.kicad_pcb`, its schematic and its project. text-to-cad reads,
draws and inspects them itself, and runs KiCad headless for everything KiCad owns: ERC, DRC, exports
and edits through its IPC API. There is no board model or build step; the files are the source.

## Start with the task

| Task | Start with | Reference |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Read a board or a schematic | `kicad_pcb.read`, `kicad_sch.read` in a script; `cad kicad_pcb inspect` | [Checks](references/checks.md), [schematic](references/schematic.md#read-it) |
| Draw or edit a schematic | `kicad_sch.edit`, then `cad kicad_sch erc` | [Schematic](references/schematic.md) |
| Choose parts and footprints | The datasheet, then the project's libraries | [Parts](references/parts.md) |
| Create or edit a board | `kicad_pcb.edit` ([below](#native-files-are-the-source)) | [Native files](references/board-api.md) |
| Place and route | The schematic's netlist, one functional group at a time | [Layout](references/layout.md), [placement](references/placement.md) |
| Check a change | `cad kicad_pcb drc`, snapshots | [Check each change](#check-each-change) |
| Review before ordering | DRC, then measurements, then the checklist | [Before ordering](#before-ordering) |
| Export fabrication files, a BOM, or a STEP for an enclosure | `cad kicad_pcb export`, `cad kicad_sch export` | [Manufacturing](references/manufacturing.md) |
| Show a board or a schematic; what the person can see or pick in it; a missing 3D model | `cad viewer --json FILE` | [Show the model](#show-the-model), [views](references/views.md) |

## Setup

Written for `cad==0.11.17`. Before first use in a chat, run `cad --version`. If `cad` is missing or older than
0.11.12, run `uv tool install cad`, adding `--force` if uv says `cad` already exists.

If cad is a major or minor version newer than this skill, tell the person to update the text-to-cad plugin:
https://github.com/earthtojake/text-to-cad
A project written for an earlier version may need changes; the migration guides say what:
https://github.com/earthtojake/text-to-cad/tree/main/docs/migrations

Reading and inspecting a board or schematic needs no KiCad. DRC, ERC, exports, edits, and drawing a
board (its copper pours are refilled on a copy first) run KiCad's own `kicad-cli` and IPC API, which
`cad` fetches the first time one is needed (kicode: about 100 MB to download, 340 MB on disk, once);
`cad run` gives a script the same. Things to know about that KiCad:

- **It is a nightly (10.99).** A file it saves is in the nightly's format, which a stable KiCad app
  refuses to open; viewing and snapshots still work, and the viewer tells the person which KiCad on
  this computer can open the file. Say so before the first save of a board the person opens in a
  stable KiCad.
- **It runs headless with private settings**, never the person's KiCad app or its settings: never open
  a board in KiCad's app to check it. A project library row that names a stock library as KiCad's own
  tables do (`${KICAD10_SYMBOL_DIR}/Device.kicad_sym`) is read from the KiCad the person installed;
  with none installed, ERC warns `lib_symbol_issues` and DRC `lib_footprint_issues`. A project that
  carries its libraries (`${KIPRJMOD}`) needs no KiCad installed.
- **An edit needs a local socket.** A shell sandbox that refuses sockets (an agent app's default) stops
  an edit at once, saying so: run the script outside the sandbox. Inspecting, DRC, exports and
  snapshots run inside it.
- **A KiCad the person installed is never run.** Where the fetched one does not run on a computer,
  `CAD_KICAD_CLI` names another `kicad-cli` (KiCad 9 or newer; a nightly's for an edit).
- **`CAD_KICAD_REFILL=0` in the server's environment turns the refill off**: showing a board then
  downloads nothing, and its pours are drawn as the file saved them.

## Native files are the source

Edit the `.kicad_pcb` itself and keep its `.kicad_pro`, `.kicad_dru`, libraries and schematic beside
it. Reading or showing a board never writes it. Reread the file before an edit, preserve records and
UUIDs you do not understand, and never regenerate an existing project from a partial description.

A board changes inside a `with` block that hands over KiPy's open `Board` and saves at the end only if
the block changed it; a block that raises saves nothing. `kicad_sch.edit` does the same for a schematic
([schematic](references/schematic.md#edit-it)). Run the script with `cad run board.py`:

```python
from cad import kicad_pcb
from kicode.util.units import from_mm

BOARD = "board.kicad_pcb"

with kicad_pcb.edit(BOARD) as b:       # the board file is the source; the block edits it in place
    power = [t for t in b.get_tracks() if t.net.name in {"+5V", "+3V3"}]
    for track in power:
        track.width = from_mm(0.8)
    b.update_items(power)
    b.refill_zones()
drc = kicad_pcb.drc(BOARD)
if not drc.ok:
    raise SystemExit("\n".join(drc.human_lines()))  # each finding, then FAILED and the count
for kind in ("gerbers", "drill", "pos", "bom", "step"):
    kicad_pcb.export(BOARD, to=kind, out=f"fab/{kind}")
```

- **State the result, not the change**: "U1 is at (10, 20)", "the power tracks are 0.8 mm", never
  "move U1 5 mm". Set absolute positions, rotations, widths and nets, and create an item only when the
  board does not hold it yet, so a script stopped halfway and run again ends where one run would.
- **Import KiPy's names from `kicode`** (`from kicode.proto.common.types import KIID`), never from
  `kipy`: the two cannot share a process.
- **Coordinates are millimetres, y down.** Footprint-local positions and rotations are transformed into
  the board frame; route to a net's actual pad positions.
- **Refill changed zones** (`b.refill_zones()`) before relying on their fill.
- KiCad's first start in a new environment can take a minute.

A board's design starts at its schematic, which says what connects to what: read it, check it with ERC
and look at each sheet before laying out, and hold the board to it after. Place one functional group at
a time, route the nets whose path matters by hand, and direct cad's router (`cad.kicad.route`, inside
the edit, with the plan you give it; never a third-party autorouter) through the rest, with widths
for each net's current ([layout](references/layout.md)). A plausible-looking layout does not
establish electrical correctness: pin numbers, footprint orientation and connector mating side come
from the datasheet.

For anything the typed commands do not cover, `cad run kicad-cli ...` runs the fetched KiCad's
command line with its own subcommands and flags (`cad run kicad-cli pcb --help`); `CAD_KICAD_CLI`
does not change which one that is:

```bash
cad run kicad-cli pcb render --side top --rotate -45,0,45 -o tmp/board.png board.kicad_pcb
cad run kicad-cli project downgrade --dry-run --target 10.0 board.kicad_pro   # then -o DIR without --dry-run
```

Most of its commands write only their `-o` (it may leave a `.kicad_prl` beside a board it reads).
These rewrite the source: `pcb upgrade`, `sch upgrade`, `fp upgrade` and `sym upgrade` without `-o`,
and `pcb drc --refill-zones --save-board`.

## Check each change

Check the saved board after every step, from the revision you will hand over:

| The change | Check it with |
| --- | --- |
| The schematic | `cad kicad_sch erc board.kicad_sch`, and `cad kicad_sch snapshot board.kicad_sch tmp/sheet.png --sheet /Power/` for each sheet changed |
| Board against schematic | The pin-by-pin comparison in [schematic](references/schematic.md#into-the-board-and-back): every pad on its schematic pin's net |
| Anything on the board | `cad kicad_pcb drc board.kicad_pcb` (`--json`): KiCad's DRC against the board's own rules. It exits 1 on errors or unconnected items; unconnected items are the routing still to do |
| Placement | `cad kicad_pcb snapshot board.kicad_pcb tmp/placement.png --display placement`: short, uncrossed ratsnest lines mean a group is placed well |
| Routing | The layout's [property script](references/layout.md#a-property-check): segments off 45 degrees, detours, width for current |
| How copper and silkscreen look | `cad kicad_pcb snapshot board.kicad_pcb tmp/copper.png --display copper` ([more views](references/views.md#board-snapshots)) |
| Ready to order | The review below |

- Warnings count: KiCad's silkscreen, mask and courtyard rules are warnings, and they are what a fab's
  CAM engineer flags.
- Fix the cause; a rule weakened to get a clean report has shown nothing.
- A clean DRC establishes the board's own rules, not the circuit's correctness and not the fab's
  limits. A number is measured from the board (`kicad_pcb.read`), never read off a snapshot.

## Before ordering

A review of one board for the fab and assembler it will be ordered from is a guided review, not the
fab's own engineering check. Gather evidence in this order: KiCad's DRC (every error blocks ordering);
then what DRC cannot measure, from the board read back and the project's BOM; then the checklist of
what no command measures.

| Area | Reference | Measured by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fabrication | [review-fabrication](references/review-fabrication.md) | KiCad's DRC against the board's rules; the rest by inspection |
| Electrical | [review-electrical](references/review-electrical.md) | The board read back: decoupling distances, narrowest track per net |
| Assembly and sourcing | [review-assembly](references/review-assembly.md) | The part list and placement file |

### Choosing the rules

Use the chosen fab's own capability page for the board's layer count, copper weight and finish, and
compare it with the project's Board Setup, which may differ. Where the person names no fab, review
against JLCPCB's standard service and say so. Record each limit's source, date and conditions; a rule
that cannot be checked is reported as missing, never invented. A fab's standard tier is a price, not a
physical limit.

### The report

Scope first (board file and revision, fab and service, layers, copper, finish, assembled or bare),
then the findings, errors first, each naming its parts by board reference (`U2`, `C8`, `#net:VBUS`;
`kicad_pcb.read(path).resolve(ref)` says where one is), with the evidence, the rule and its source,
the result and the fix. Then the coverage: checks run, and checks not run with what they need.

| Item | Evidence | Rule | Result | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `U2` pad 3 to `C8` | measured 3.67 mm centre to centre from the board read back | decoupling within 3 mm (this review's guide) | review | move `C8` beside pin 3 |

The result is **pass** (measured, within a cited limit), **fail** (a measured violation or a KiCad
error), **review** (a risk a person decides) or **unverified** (evidence or the fab's rule is missing).
No findings is not a manufacturability approval. A review alone asks for no edits: fix only when
asked, and recheck the neighbours of every fix.

Export only the deliverables asked for, from the revision you checked
([manufacturing](references/manufacturing.md)). A DRC or ERC error blocks writing fabrication files
unless the person says to go ahead, and the report then names every error they went ahead with.

## Show the model

Show the person each model you create or change as soon as its first run succeeds, and any model
or file they ask to see. A model's page is the `view:` line its run prints, and a file's is the `url`
that `cad viewer --json FILE [FILE ...]` prints for it (never guess the port). Show it with
the first of these you have:

1. `cad_show` among your tools (your host may prefix it): call it with the model's id or the file's
   absolute path; its description says the rest.
2. A tool that opens a page in the app's own browser pane, not in the person's own browser (in the
   Claude desktop app, the Browser pane's `preview_start` with the page's `url`, or its `navigate`):
   open the page there yourself, and give the person the link as well.
3. Neither: give the person the link, to open in their browser.

The page follows every run of the model. A file you export is a download: give its path. Showing is
for the person: to check your own work, review with `cad <type> snapshot`, never a screenshot
of the page. If it fails to launch, say so.

What the board and schematic pages offer the person (layers, selection, 3D, part models), and what
they approximate, is in [views](references/views.md).

# PCB design

A board is its native KiCad files: the `.kicad_pcb`, its schematic and its project. text-to-cad reads,
draws and inspects them itself, and runs KiCad headless for everything KiCad owns: ERC, DRC, exports
and edits through its IPC API. There is no board model or build step; the files are the source.

## Start with the task

| Task | Start with | Reference |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Read a board or a schematic | `kicad_pcb.read`, `kicad_sch.read` in a script; `cad kicad_pcb inspect` | [Checks](references/checks.md), [schematic](references/schematic.md#read-it) |
| Draw or edit a schematic | `kicad_sch.edit`, then `cad kicad_sch erc` | [Schematic](references/schematic.md) |
| Choose parts and footprints | The datasheet, then the project's libraries | [Parts](references/parts.md) |
| Create or edit a board | `kicad_pcb.edit` ([below](#native-files-are-the-source)) | [Native files](references/board-api.md) |
| Place and route | The schematic's netlist, one functional group at a time | [Layout](references/layout.md), [placement](references/placement.md) |
| Check a change | `cad kicad_pcb drc`, snapshots | [Check each change](#check-each-change) |
| Review before ordering | DRC, then measurements, then the checklist | [Before ordering](#before-ordering) |
| Export fabrication files, a BOM, or a STEP for an enclosure | `cad kicad_pcb export`, `cad kicad_sch export` | [Manufacturing](references/manufacturing.md) |
| Show a board or a schematic; what the person can see or pick in it; a missing 3D model | `cad viewer --json FILE` | [Show the model](#show-the-model), [views](references/views.md) |

## Setup

Written for `cad==0.11.17`. Before first use in a chat, run `cad --version`. If `cad` is missing or older than
0.11.12, run `uv tool install cad`, adding `--force` if uv says `cad` already exists.

If cad is a major or minor version newer than this skill, tell the person to update the text-to-cad plugin:
https://github.com/earthtojake/text-to-cad
A project written for an earlier version may need changes; the migration guides say what:
https://github.com/earthtojake/text-to-cad/tree/main/docs/migrations

Reading and inspecting a board or schematic needs no KiCad. DRC, ERC, exports, edits, and drawing a
board (its copper pours are refilled on a copy first) run KiCad's own `kicad-cli` and IPC API, which
`cad` fetches the first time one is needed (kicode: about 100 MB to download, 340 MB on disk, once);
`cad run` gives a script the same. Things to know about that KiCad:

- **It is a nightly (10.99).** A file it saves is in the nightly's format, which a stable KiCad app
  refuses to open; viewing and snapshots still work, and the viewer tells the person which KiCad on
  this computer can open the file. Say so before the first save of a board the person opens in a
  stable KiCad.
- **It runs headless with private settings**, never the person's KiCad app or its settings: never open
  a board in KiCad's app to check it. A project library row that names a stock library as KiCad's own
  tables do (`${KICAD10_SYMBOL_DIR}/Device.kicad_sym`) is read from the KiCad the person installed;
  with none installed, ERC warns `lib_symbol_issues` and DRC `lib_footprint_issues`. A project that
  carries its libraries (`${KIPRJMOD}`) needs no KiCad installed.
- **An edit needs a local socket.** A shell sandbox that refuses sockets (an agent app's default) stops
  an edit at once, saying so: run the script outside the sandbox. Inspecting, DRC, exports and
  snapshots run inside it.
- **A KiCad the person installed is never run.** Where the fetched one does not run on a computer,
  `CAD_KICAD_CLI` names another `kicad-cli` (KiCad 9 or newer; a nightly's for an edit).
- **`CAD_KICAD_REFILL=0` in the server's environment turns the refill off**: showing a board then
  downloads nothing, and its pours are drawn as the file saved them.

## Native files are the source

Edit the `.kicad_pcb` itself and keep its `.kicad_pro`, `.kicad_dru`, libraries and schematic beside
it. Reading or showing a board never writes it. Reread the file before an edit, preserve records and
UUIDs you do not understand, and never regenerate an existing project from a partial description.

A board changes inside a `with` block that hands over KiPy's open `Board` and saves at the end only if
the block changed it; a block that raises saves nothing. `kicad_sch.edit` does the same for a schematic
([schematic](references/schematic.md#edit-it)). Run the script with `cad run board.py`:

```python
from cad import kicad_pcb
from kicode.util.units import from_mm

BOARD = "board.kicad_pcb"

with kicad_pcb.edit(BOARD) as b:       # the board file is the source; the block edits it in place
    power = [t for t in b.get_tracks() if t.net.name in {"+5V", "+3V3"}]
    for track in power:
        track.width = from_mm(0.8)
    b.update_items(power)
    b.refill_zones()
drc = kicad_pcb.drc(BOARD)
if not drc.ok:
    raise SystemExit("\n".join(drc.human_lines()))  # each finding, then FAILED and the count
for kind in ("gerbers", "drill", "pos", "bom", "step"):
    kicad_pcb.export(BOARD, to=kind, out=f"fab/{kind}")
```

- **State the result, not the change**: "U1 is at (10, 20)", "the power tracks are 0.8 mm", never
  "move U1 5 mm". Set absolute positions, rotations, widths and nets, and create an item only when the
  board does not hold it yet, so a script stopped halfway and run again ends where one run would.
- **Import KiPy's names from `kicode`** (`from kicode.proto.common.types import KIID`), never from
  `kipy`: the two cannot share a process.
- **Coordinates are millimetres, y down.** Footprint-local positions and rotations are transformed into
  the board frame; route to a net's actual pad positions.
- **Refill changed zones** (`b.refill_zones()`) before relying on their fill.
- KiCad's first start in a new environment can take a minute.

A board's design starts at its schematic, which says what connects to what: read it, check it with ERC
and look at each sheet before laying out, and hold the board to it after. Place one functional group at
a time, route the nets whose path matters by hand, and direct cad's router (`cad.kicad.route`, inside
the edit, with the plan you give it; never a third-party autorouter) through the rest, with widths
for each net's current ([layout](references/layout.md)). A plausible-looking layout does not
establish electrical correctness: pin numbers, footprint orientation and connector mating side come
from the datasheet.

For anything the typed commands do not cover, `cad run kicad-cli ...` runs the fetched KiCad's
command line with its own subcommands and flags (`cad run kicad-cli pcb --help`); `CAD_KICAD_CLI`
does not change which one that is:

```bash
cad run kicad-cli pcb render --side top --rotate -45,0,45 -o tmp/board.png board.kicad_pcb
cad run kicad-cli project downgrade --dry-run --target 10.0 board.kicad_pro   # then -o DIR without --dry-run
```

Most of its commands write only their `-o` (it may leave a `.kicad_prl` beside a board it reads).
These rewrite the source: `pcb upgrade`, `sch upgrade`, `fp upgrade` and `sym upgrade` without `-o`,
and `pcb drc --refill-zones --save-board`.

## Check each change

Check the saved board after every step, from the revision you will hand over:

| The change | Check it with |
| --- | --- |
| The schematic | `cad kicad_sch erc board.kicad_sch`, and `cad kicad_sch snapshot board.kicad_sch tmp/sheet.png --sheet /Power/` for each sheet changed |
| Board against schematic | The pin-by-pin comparison in [schematic](references/schematic.md#into-the-board-and-back): every pad on its schematic pin's net |
| Anything on the board | `cad kicad_pcb drc board.kicad_pcb` (`--json`): KiCad's DRC against the board's own rules. It exits 1 on errors or unconnected items; unconnected items are the routing still to do |
| Placement | `cad kicad_pcb snapshot board.kicad_pcb tmp/placement.png --display placement`: short, uncrossed ratsnest lines mean a group is placed well |
| Routing | The layout's [property script](references/layout.md#a-property-check): segments off 45 degrees, detours, width for current |
| How copper and silkscreen look | `cad kicad_pcb snapshot board.kicad_pcb tmp/copper.png --display copper` ([more views](references/views.md#board-snapshots)) |
| Ready to order | The review below |

- Warnings count: KiCad's silkscreen, mask and courtyard rules are warnings, and they are what a fab's
  CAM engineer flags.
- Fix the cause; a rule weakened to get a clean report has shown nothing.
- A clean DRC establishes the board's own rules, not the circuit's correctness and not the fab's
  limits. A number is measured from the board (`kicad_pcb.read`), never read off a snapshot.

## Before ordering

A review of one board for the fab and assembler it will be ordered from is a guided review, not the
fab's own engineering check. Gather evidence in this order: KiCad's DRC (every error blocks ordering);
then what DRC cannot measure, from the board read back and the project's BOM; then the checklist of
what no command measures.

| Area | Reference | Measured by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fabrication | [review-fabrication](references/review-fabrication.md) | KiCad's DRC against the board's rules; the rest by inspection |
| Electrical | [review-electrical](references/review-electrical.md) | The board read back: decoupling distances, narrowest track per net |
| Assembly and sourcing | [review-assembly](references/review-assembly.md) | The part list and placement file |

### Choosing the rules

Use the chosen fab's own capability page for the board's layer count, copper weight and finish, and
compare it with the project's Board Setup, which may differ. Where the person names no fab, review
against JLCPCB's standard service and say so. Record each limit's source, date and conditions; a rule
that cannot be checked is reported as missing, never invented. A fab's standard tier is a price, not a
physical limit.

### The report

Scope first (board file and revision, fab and service, layers, copper, finish, assembled or bare),
then the findings, errors first, each naming its parts by board reference (`U2`, `C8`, `#net:VBUS`;
`kicad_pcb.read(path).resolve(ref)` says where one is), with the evidence, the rule and its source,
the result and the fix. Then the coverage: checks run, and checks not run with what they need.

| Item | Evidence | Rule | Result | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `U2` pad 3 to `C8` | measured 3.67 mm centre to centre from the board read back | decoupling within 3 mm (this review's guide) | review | move `C8` beside pin 3 |

The result is **pass** (measured, within a cited limit), **fail** (a measured violation or a KiCad
error), **review** (a risk a person decides) or **unverified** (evidence or the fab's rule is missing).
No findings is not a manufacturability approval. A review alone asks for no edits: fix only when
asked, and recheck the neighbours of every fix.

Export only the deliverables asked for, from the revision you checked
([manufacturing](references/manufacturing.md)). A DRC or ERC error blocks writing fabrication files
unless the person says to go ahead, and the report then names every error they went ahead with.

## Show the model

Show the person each model you create or change as soon as its first run succeeds, and any model
or file they ask to see. A model's page is the `view:` line its run prints, and a file's is the `url`
that `cad viewer --json FILE [FILE ...]` prints for it (never guess the port). Show it with
the first of these you have:

1. `cad_show` among your tools (your host may prefix it): call it with the model's id or the file's
   absolute path; its description says the rest.
2. A tool that opens a page in the app's own browser pane, not in the person's own browser (in the
   Claude desktop app, the Browser pane's `preview_start` with the page's `url`, or its `navigate`):
   open the page there yourself, and give the person the link as well.
3. Neither: give the person the link, to open in their browser.

The page follows every run of the model. A file you export is a download: give its path. Showing is
for the person: to check your own work, review with `cad <type> snapshot`, never a screenshot
of the page. If it fails to launch, say so.

What the board and schematic pages offer the person (layers, selection, 3D, part models), and what
they approximate, is in [views](references/views.md).
